BreakingNewsTab.title: Princess of Wales: Catherine talks about her cancer journey in new documentary Heal
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

Catherine has never disclosed what type of cancer she faced, but in March 2024 she revealed that she had a diagnosis of cancer and was receiving chemotherapy.

In January 2025 she announced that she was in remission and in the following months began a gradual return to royal duties.

She has often spoken about her different understanding of life after her illness, and the need to take a more holistic approach to well-being beyond physical recovery.

The princess has talked about the good days and bad days that followed her treatment - and wanted to dispel the idea that patients could immediately return to how they felt before their illness.

This documentary, which will be introduced by Kirsty Young, promises to be the fullest and most personal account of that journey, with her own insights into the impact such illness can have and how she found her own healing process.

She has since returned to working for her charities and earlier this week was in India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with Prince William, the first time they had travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.

"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.

"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.

"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."

The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.

Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.

Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Wales 26-29 Australia: Wallabies hold on for Nations Championship win in Cardiff
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Nations Championship

Tries: Lake 2, Murray, Elias Cons: Costelow 3

Tries: Tupou, Paenga-Amosa, Jorgensen, Ikitau Cons: Lonergan 2, Gordon Pens: Gordon

Wales could not emulate their famous victory against New Zealand as Australia claimed the Nations Championship spoils in Cardiff.

The Wallabies ended a four-match losing run thanks to tries from hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa, prop Taniela Tupou, wing Max Jorgensen and centre Len Ikitau, while fly-half Carter Gordon kicked a late penalty.

Wales captain Dewi Lake scored two tries, while full-back Blair Murray also crossed following a superb assist by wing Louis Rees-Zammit.

Replacement hooker Ryan Elias grabbed a late try but Australia held on for victory as Wales paid the price for not capitalising on attacking chances.

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere section and will play Japan at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table and play Ireland on Friday (20:10 GMT).

After all the hysteria and celebrations to mark a first victory against the All Blacks in 73 years, the attention turned towards whether Wales could back it up against Australia.

There was a vibrancy on the streets of Cardiff before the game not seen for a while, which reflected in the crowd.

After crowds of 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand, the 66,307 attendance against Australia was the highest of the autumn.

The All Blacks win proved instrumental in a surge of tickets sold for a 20:10 GMT kick-off, the latest for a Wales rugby home game at the Principality Stadium.

Head coach Steve Tandy made four changes to revert to the side that beat Japan with flanker James Botham the most notable absentee following his player-of-the-match against New Zealand.

Botham was expecting the birth of his first child this week but Tandy stated his omission was for rugby reasons with Cardiff colleague Alex Mann replacing him.

Fit-again number eight Aaron Wainwright replaced Taine Basham, while lock Ben Carter and wing Josh Adams returned for Adam Beard and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.

Australia had freshened things up with five forward changes as flanker Carlo Tizzano, lock Tom Hooper and the front-row trio of Isaac Kailea, Paenga-Amosa and Tupou came in.

Wales lost centre Max Llewellyn inside two minutes to a yellow card for a high tackle on Wallabies full-back Tom Wright.

Wallabies had plenty of early possession against 14 players but the home defence comfortably dealt with the attack.

Mann was caught with some friendly fire by a finger in the eye from team-mate Carter but continued despite appearing to have vision issues.

Rees-Zammit almost squeezed into the corner but just failed to ground the ball under pressure from Gordon, before Lake was held up over the Australia line.

Mann, despite his eye seeming to be closing, was still able to force a turnover penalty but Wales were guilty of early handling errors.

After Wales won a scrum penalty, the officials then either missed Tupou striking Mann with a body jab, or deemed it did not warrant further action.

Tupou stayed on the field to open the scoring in the 21st minute as he evaded Llewellyn's tackle to cross for an unconverted try.

Wales retaliated quickly with Morgan breaking away and feeding scrum-half Tomos Williams, who was held up by superb visiting defence.

There were important turnover penalties from Tizzano and Tupou who benefitted from a huge tackle from Australia captain Harry Wilson on opposite number Wainwright.

The hosts held the upper hand in the first-half aerial battle but Wales were not as clinical as they were against New Zealand.

Australia centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii gained an intercept before being hauled down by Rees-Zammit, who conceded a penalty.

Wallabies demonstrated a more ruthless approach as Paenga-Amosa was driven over.

Mann continued to wind up the Australia forwards, which helped gain 10 metres for dissent, but Wales continued to waste chances as an attacking line-out was stolen.

Morgan was a Wales carrying colossus in the first half with a series of impressive bursts and the home side finally gained a reward in the 40th minute when Lake dived over with Costelow converting.

Australia led 12-7 at half-time with Wales having an on-pitch huddle before heading to their changing room.

Australia brought on experienced forward replacements with Fraser McReight and Angus Bell making immediate impacts.

Prop Allan Alaalatoa appeared to have scored on his 99th international, but it was ruled out following a knock-on by replacement scrum-half Kalani Thomas.

The Wallabies wave continued with Wales duo Eddie James and Archie Griffin producing impressive tackles before Ikitau restored the visitors' lead.

Morgan left the field for a head injury assessment (HIA) to be replaced by Kane James, who was in tears when the anthem was played as he marked his first Wales appearance in Cardiff.

Fellow replacement Louie Hennessey knocked on to give Australia an attacking platform before Wainwright conceded a penalty which Carter kicked to take the Wallabies two scores clear.

Morgan returned and Wales responded as they battered the Australia line with Wilson shown a yellow card.

Elias was driven over to secure two losing bonus-points and set up a grandstand finale, but Wallabies held on for a vital victory for head coach Les Kiss.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

BreakingNewsTab.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".

"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.

But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.

They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".

After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.

Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.

Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.

During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".

Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".

The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.

While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.

She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.

Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.

But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.

"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door.

"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"

The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.

Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.

He remains behind bars awaiting trial.

A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.

"Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away."

"She's doing great for what she's gone through."

They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.

"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

BreakingNewsTab.title: AI is being used to clone real people's videos
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.

But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.

From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.

Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.

Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.

"A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we've created," says Sophie Lloyd, a UK-based guitarist who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, who has spent years building a successful online presence.

Lloyd says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.

BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person. The videos on the Vasari account also contain visual inconsistencies that suggest AI was used to create them, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music, and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed.

The account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos. Its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify has found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content.

But Lloyd is far from alone in having her content manipulated by AI.

"I've got so many messages from other artists and creators that have had the same thing happening to them," says Kjetil Krogstad, a Norwegian content creator known for videos showing him happily dancing in a suit while carrying a cup of tea.

In March, his followers alerted him to the fact that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny. The post went on to attract millions of views - outperforming Krogstad's original video - before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.

Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money.

"What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that's already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools," she says.

Kendall sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture", in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money - be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms.

And making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, Kendall says. "That's the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful, it really conforms with these conventional cultural ideals of attractiveness, success, aspiration, beauty."

Dozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission.

"I cannot explain how angry I am right now," Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram. "Someone not only stole my video, but also changed me into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and this is literally my job," she said, showing the original video of herself wearing jeans, smiling and covering her ears at a drag car race next to an AI-generated version with a blonde woman in a short dress.

"I put the videos side by side and I could see it was my exact facial movements, how my body moved, the exact same background and even the people around me were completely copied," she told BBC Verify. "It was just me that had been altered."

"I pay for the cars, I build the cars, I pay for the cameras, the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and then make money off the back of my video," she added.

Her concerns are echoed by other content creators who fear these AI-generated accounts could cost them valuable exposure, followers, and potential income.

American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video: "The thing that is most concerning is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they're real people.

"And for context, comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy," she said, adding that comedians spent a long time crafting jokes on stage and honing them into punchy lines.

Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate.

But legal protections are only part of the challenge. Identifying those responsible for copying the videos, and stopping them from doing it again, can also prove difficult.

Stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole, says Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians. "You don't even know who's making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they're just going to create another," he says.

"It's not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I've seen this all over the internet."

Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this.

Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also "working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals".

But for artists like Lloyd, the damage may already be done. "It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else - and then people don't even know it's you."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not.

"I've spent all that time and energy submitting my application but got nothing in return."

Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.

The 24-year-old says her biggest challenge throughout the job-hunting process has been not getting feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.

She says she has also been ghosted after interviews several times.

"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.

Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.

"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, a 21-year-old, from Swindon.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Newspaper headlines: Kate's 'road to recovery' and 'Brave princess'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Mail on Sunday reports, external the Prince of Wales may strip his brother the Duke of Sussex of his titles when he becomes king, according to an upcoming book. Citing the royal author Tom Sykes, the paper says Prince William is planning a "radical shake-up of the monarchy", which would include HRH titles only being granted to working royals. A spokesperson for the Prince and Catherine, Princess of Wales said they do not comment on claims made in books.

Several front pages feature photos of Kate ahead of next weekend's BBC documentary in which she discusses her cancer recovery. The Daily Star Sunday, external describes her as "our queen of hearts", saying she has used her public profile "to raise money and awareness" for others. The Sunday Telegraph, external describes her as "grinning and winning" - a reference to her Three Peaks hiking challenge for charity.

Lord Blunkett has a warning for Andy Burnham in the Sun on Sunday, external - after the prime minister moved to forge closer ties with the European Union on Friday. The former Labour minister describes himself as "sceptical", arguing that "the electorate are not yet ready for even bolder moves to integration". Alan Johnson, who launched Labour's 2016 campaign to remain in the EU, has a similar warning for the prime minister in the Sunday Mirror, external. He tells the paper another referendum "would be very damaging".

The Sunday Times leads, external on its joint investigation with the BBC into the case of a man who killed three people in Exeter while suffering from a psychotic episode in 2019. The paper says the victims were "killed after police incompetence" - as warnings about the man's behaviour were ignored. Devon and Cornwall police says it is addressing "areas of learning".

The late author, Dame Jilly Cooper, is accused of plagiarism in claims carried by the Observer, external. The paper says a "detailed analysis" of her fifth book "Prudence" shows that she copiously plundered two other novels - The Serial by Cyra McFadden and Josephine Tey's The Franchise Affair. Her agent and publisher did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock and have been suspended for the night, after running more than a day over time, as countries have been unable to agree on a new global climate deal.

The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.

Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.

If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.

In that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

On Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."

The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.

"These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together."

Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.

He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - was the biggest contributor to meeting new global energy demand, outstripping oil and gas, external.

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War continues, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.

Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.

It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.

This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed.

"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as co-hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", said one observer.

BreakingNewsTab.title: 'El Chapo Isidro': Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.

Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.

Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.

Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.

The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.

It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.

When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.

Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.

He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.

The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.

FinanceTab.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

FinanceTab.title: Andy Burnham: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal
FinanceTab.text:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

FinanceTab.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
FinanceTab.text:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

FinanceTab.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
FinanceTab.text:
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.

Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.

The latest official sales figures, external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.

"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.

"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."

The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September.

As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.

FinanceTab.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
FinanceTab.text:
There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.

In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.

A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.

However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.

"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.

"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

FinanceTab.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
FinanceTab.text:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

FinanceTab.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
FinanceTab.text:
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.

The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.

A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.

About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.

Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".

The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.

Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.

But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.

He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.

According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.

But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".

In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.

It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.

However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.

Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."

While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.

The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties.

"The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.

Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.

He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.

Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.

Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.

Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".

He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.

Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.

Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".

It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.

Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".

In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats.

Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.

Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure".

"Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.

The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.

None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.

Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented.

"It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."
