FinanceTab.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

"AI carries real risks," she added.

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
FinanceTab.text:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

FinanceTab.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
FinanceTab.text:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

FinanceTab.title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
FinanceTab.text:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.

Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more.

The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid.

Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job.

The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US.

“The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement.

Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto, which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018.

The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, ‌but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims.

Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades ​of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer.

The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under ⁠state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits.

Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for ​many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell ​decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims ​to pursue claims in court.

“We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all ​Roundup victims as quickly ‌as possible,” he ​said in a statement.

Lawyers for ​some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

SportsTab.title: England 37-12 New Zealand: Can win over All Blacks finally break boom-bust cycle?
SportsTab.text:
We have been here before of course.

Twelve months ago, as today, England took a famous win over New Zealand.

After a run of victories against lesser opponents, it was the litmus test of their progress. They passed with flying colours and a comfortable scoreline.

It was a statement victory, a sign of things to come. England were building into world-beaters.

The similarities to today's 37-12 success are striking. Even the attendance figure - 81,953 - matches.

For England fans, burned by the dismal Six Nations that followed the 2025 result, there will be a shot of caution with the celebratory drinks tonight.

Steve Borthwick's four-year reign has been marked by booms and busts.

Five defeats in six Tests preceded the 2023 Rugby World Cup, when they came within a point of making the final.

They lost five straight matches in the back half of 2024, before embarking on 12-Test winning streak at the start of 2025.

The sunny uplands have too often turned out to be false dawns.

But, there are grounds to think this time, just maybe, is different.

For a start, it is a different England team, playing a different way.

When the team was named on Thursday, it was striking that England's backline contained none of the same starters as 12 months ago.

Steward, Roebuck, Lawrence, Dingwall, Feyi-Waboso, Ford and Mitchell read the teamsheet for the 2025 win over New Zealand.

Furbank, Murley, Slade, Atkinson, Joseph, Smith, and Van Poortvliet was its 2026 equivalent.

But for injury, Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Alex Mitchell may have featured in both. Tommy Freeman likewise.

But the balance has shifted.

The class of 2026, with Fin Smith pulling strings, Henry Slade distributing to pace out wide, and George Furbank out the back and at first receiver, is a more fluid unit.

Seb Atkinson, up against Jordie Barrett, was critical to England's variety, able to combine full-throated midfield carries with deft hands.

In part, it is horses for courses.

Twelve months ago, kicking and chasing was in vogue. And England were setting the trend.

In their 2025 win over the All Blacks, England put boot to ball 35 times and passed it 104 times. A ratio of one to three.

This time around, the stat showed 29 kicks to 176 passes. The boot is being used half as much in relative terms.

The change has been forced to a degree. After a law tweak initially made the aerial route profitable last year, defences have found ways to counter, with retreating catchers and pockets of players posted to pick up scraps.

England had to find new dimensions. And they have.

Jack van Poortvliet and Ollie Chessum's tries were created by clever movement and midfield breaks by Cadan Murley and Will Joseph respectively.

From similar positions 12 months ago, England would have been tempted to take to the skies.

The current way of playing is less predictable, and more sustainable as a long-term tactic to threaten the game's superpowers at the backend of next year's Rugby World Cup.

The balance of power up front has tilted further in England's favour as well.

New Zealand were without talismanic captain Ardie Savea and fellow forwards Luke Jacobsen and Shannon Frizell. But still, England's heavy traffic ram-raided through the heart of the visiting pack a startling number of times.

Ben Earl particularly had a field day. The number eight has been a star performer throughout his team's fluctuating form and stamped his authority on this contest with a whopping 33 carries and 138 metres made.

Ellis Genge, Greg Fisilau and George Martin were abrasive off the bench, cementing England's advantage.

Defensively, England were tight.

Twelve months ago, New Zealand leapt out into a 12-0 lead with two tries in the first 17 minutes. They never looked like piling on points in a similar quickfire way this time around.

The visitors had only three line breaks compared to nine in 2025.

The dominance was near total. The All Blacks were all out of answers.

And England would have been out of sight sooner with a fewer errors in the first half.

"It was a very good performance and what's exciting is we left some points out there - I think we can be even better," Borthwick told BBC Radio 5 Live afterwards.

"No journey of a team is ever linear. There are always ups and downs that you work through. We continue to strive to improve.

"This is a team that has got enormous growth in it and I'm excited about the journey.

"If players keep the attitude they have to want to get better - and you can see that with the defence, because it was a brilliant defensive performance - when you have that level of commitment, what the players can achieve, I'm excited by the possibilities."

England's fans have certainly bought in.

Lewis Moody's appearance alongside the team for the haka, after presenting them their shirts the previous evening, was an invite to emotionally invest that was impossible to turn down.

The manner in which England's players, in the seconds before kick-off, sought Moody out to embrace him spoke of a bond.

The crowd responded to something special and real.

The All Blacks, famed aura faded, were reduced to minor roles.

Beaten last weekend by Wales, their long season is in severe danger of fizzling out.

If so, it is understandable. They have been set the most brutal of schedules.

In the aftermath of July's Nations Championship they have played nine Tests in less than three months. Four of those were away to South Africa, with the final meeting in the Greatest Rivalry series staged in Baltimore to add a few more air miles to their dizzying itinerary.

Battle-hardened can turn to over-cooked quickly. And with Ruben Love, Quinn Tupaea, Caleb Clarke and Leroy Carter out, their backline is as patched up as their pack.

After a superb start to his All Blacks reign, Dave Rennie would be forgiven for wanted to recuperate and regroup.

As it is, his side will be back at Allianz Stadium for a rematch against England in the Nations Championship third-place play-off next Saturday.

There are big Tests down the road for Borthwick's side. Ireland away in the opening round of the Six Nations in February looms large.

But they are measuring up well, compared to their own high watermarks, as well as the rest of the Test game.

SportsTab.title: David Raya injury: Goalkeeper taken off during Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal
SportsTab.text:
Injuries are never good news, but Arsenal's latest one to first-choice goalkeeper David Raya has come in the worst possible position.

The 31-year-old was forced to leave the pitch 70 minutes into Saturday's 2-2 draw with Newcastle, appearing to hurt his shoulder in an innocuous challenge with Magpies forward William Osula.

The Gunners arguably have the best depth in the league with at least two quality options in all outfield positions after a period of squad strengthening.

In goal, however, cover appears much thinner.

Raya was a key component in Arsenal's Premier League title-winning campaign last season, was named in the Fifpro Men's World 11 and was unlucky to not win the Yashin Trophy, awarded to the world's best goalkeeper, which went to Spain team-mate Unai Simon.

Behind him, Kepa Arrizabalaga still holds the record as the most expensive goalkeeper in football history following his £72m move from Athletic Bilbao to Chelsea in August 2018, but is far behind Raya in terms of quality.

Raya's passing range and ability on the ball are key to how Arsenal build their attacks, and his presence is a big reason why they have the best defence in the league.

They have conceded just seven Premier League goals this season, with only Brighton able to match that tally - having played a game fewer.

Arsenal also brought in former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier on a free transfer in the summer but his only appearance this season came in the embarrassing Carabao Cup defeat by League Two Fleetwood.

When asked about Raya's injury, Arteta said he did not know how severe the issue is.

"Well, unfortunately, he had to come off, which is never good news," said Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta.

"He will get assessed now, and probably he will have an MRI [scan] tomorrow to see what it is exactly he has done.

"I don't know how it happened, and what the injury is at the moment, so we'll have to wait and see tomorrow."

Arsenal are about to enter a gruelling period of games - with or without Raya.

In the next four weeks, they face Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City, Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid.

"The one player that Arsenal cannot afford to lose is David Raya," said former England forward Alan Shearer, who is a pundit on Saturday's BBC Match of the Day. "He has made such a difference since joining from Brentford in 2023.

"They have top-class cover in just about every other position but he is the one individual that Mikel Arteta will be thinking 'we don't want to play without him for an extended period'. They could, of course go into the transfer market if they need to in January, but Arteta will be desperately hoping Raya is not out for long."

Raya is reportedly close to agreeing a new deal at the club, which shows his importance to the Gunners with two years remaining on his contract.

Ex-England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said on Sky Sports that Raya is "irreplaceable".

"Kepa is not up to the level of him - I actually think he struggles in the Premier League," added Redknapp. "Obviously we've seen in the Carabao Cup last year in the final.

"He is now going to have to play some games and that's going to be difficult for him.

"It will change everything for Arsenal for a while so that's a massive blow depending on how long David Raya is out because he is irreplaceable - probably the best goalkeeper in the Premier League, if not one of the best in the world."

SportsTab.title: Nations Championship: Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable with 20-17 win over South Africa
SportsTab.text:
After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get back to the levels they had reached when considered squarely among that group.

Because they had got there before came the typically uncomplicated response from the side's head coach.

The longer the 2023 World Cup receded into memory, however, fewer and fewer believed that his side still had within them the type of performance they produced to beat the Springboks 20-17 on Saturday.

Undoubtedly Ireland's biggest win of recent years, having not beaten one of the three sides who started this weekend above them in the rankings since the summer of 2024, this was one of their most needed too.

This Test had long been viewed as one of the crucial measuring sticks for Farrell's side building towards next autumn's World Cup - the last time they will face the back-to-back champions before boarding the plane to Australia.

Having settled into a pattern where they could not beat the best, but almost always found a way past the rest, Ireland could not have headed down under with genuine belief of making history without first showing they were still capable of this level.

"It's something that we've been looking forward to, to challenge ourselves and delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell.

"We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best by a stretch at this moment in time

"It was a game that we we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and, obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did, and coming out on the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who is Irish."

For all that had gone on in the build-up, from explosive news conferences to coaching suspensions, from dismissed citing complaints to eye-catching positional switches, by the time of kick-off, it almost felt as if a reminder was needed that there was still a game to be played.

Some two hours later, with the banned Rassie Erasmsus having watched on from a nearby hotel with only a host of virtual followers on a near-silent YouTube stream for company, his Springboks side had lost consecutive games for the first time in four years.

If his comments this week were designed to illicit a response from his side after last week's loss to France, he did not get the desired reaction. Instead, it was Ireland who it seemed had appropriately fuelled the fire.

Virtually scrummaged off the park in this fixture last year, prop Andrew Porter was among those who said that day had stuck with them in the months since.

While the tables were not turned at scrum-time, rather than allow the set-piece to again become the dominant thread of the game, this time around Ireland weathered the storm and came out the other side.

Their aerial work in particular was key, with Farrell typically highlighting Robert Baloucoune's efforts to regather possession before mentioning the winger's second double in as many weeks.

"We were very good at just getting on with it," added the head coach.

"It's not always going to go your way against the world's best, certainly at scrum-time, they're world-leading in that regard. We took everything in isolation and just kept going on to the next moment.

"That was the story of the game, really."

Even if South Africa had wrestled the game back in those frantic closing moments, this would not have been a loss to catalogue alongside the others against South Africa, France and New Zealand in recent years.

Having started 2026 with their intent questioned after defeat in Paris, Ireland played their last home game of the year showing an appreciation that in these sorts of contests, it is the small moments that make for big results.

A first-half scrum penalty of their own was greeted as raucously as a score while, whether it be a Joe McCarthy maul turnover, Mack Hansen's try-saving tackle on Canan Moodie or Hugo Keenan eating up the ground to thwart Kurt-Lee Arendse, Ireland continued to show that this time they were to stay in the fight.

There will still be talk of whether this was truly Ireland absorbing South Africa's best punch - with both the Boks and All Blacks having lost twice in succession, questions will be asked of how much the four-Test Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series has taken out of both sides.

"We're not playing to our best potential," said captain Siya Kolisi.

"We know as a group we have better. I don't question the effort or the mindset, but it's executing better."

Still, Ireland must believe that this was a game that said more about themselves than their opponents.

SportsTab.title: France 45-17 Argentina - Les Bleus secure final spot
SportsTab.text:
Nations Championship

Tries: Guillard, Mauvaka, Gourgues 2, Gailleton, Duguid, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Gourgues 5

Tries: Piccardo, Matera Cons: Albornoz 2 Pen: Albornoz

France dispatched Argentina in Paris to book their spot against South Africa in the Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium next Sunday.

Knowing pre-game a bonus-point victory at Stade de France would be enough to edge England out of the top spot in the northern hemisphere standings, Les Bleus had to work hard to secure the points required.

Lock Mickael Guillard powered over for the opening score, but Justo Piccardo responded for the visitors before Tomas Albornoz nudged them ahead with a penalty.

Argentina have not been at their best this November, suffering a heavy defeat by Ireland before narrowly beating Italy.

However, as is often the case with the Pumas, the longer they spend together, the more they tend to improve as a campaign progresses.

Felipe Contepomi's side brought the first-half physicality needed to trouble France, who turned to their maul late in the first half to score through Peato Mauvaka and reclaim the lead.

Fly-half Matthieu Jalibert, who missed the win over the world champions through injury, then expertly sent Kalvin Gourgues through a gap to score.

The pivotal moment came when Argentina prop Mayco Vivas was shown a 20-minute red card for making direct head contact at a ruck, with France capitalising on the extra man to score their bonus-point try through Emilien Gailleton.

Hooker Julian Montoya then joined Vivas in the sin-bin after receiving a yellow card and France made their numerical advantage count once again as Tyler Duguid and Gourgues crossed.

Pablo Matera intercepted Louis Bielle-Biarrey's pass to improve the scoreline but Bielle-Biarrey made amends to dot down a brilliant kick into space by Antoine Dupont.

It will now be rematch of last Friday's epic game in Paris, which France narrowly won 21-19 against the world champions.

South Africa booked their spot in the final by picking up a losing bonus point against Ireland.

Scotland will play Argentina on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in the seventh/eighth-place play-off.

SportsTab.title: Chelsea 1-4 Leeds: Xabi Alonso's honeymoon period appears to be over
SportsTab.text:
Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso is already in firefighting mode.

His team were booed by their own supporters at several points during a dominant 4-1 Leeds victory at Stamford Bridge, their first win there since 1999.

The first negative reaction came at half-time while the score was still 1-1. The ground then began to empty after the third and fourth Leeds goals, and the fans remaining voiced their dissent once more at the final whistle.

Although there were mitigating circumstances, including a potentially harsh penalty decision against them and the loss of midfielder Moises Caicedo to injury, joining a five-strong list of players on the treatment table, the defeat was thoroughly deserved.

It leaves Chelsea with three losses in their past four Premier League matches and they have slipped from fifth place to eighth, already 14 points behind league leaders Arsenal.

In October, Tottenham won at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the Premier League era, while the 1-0 defeat at bottom club Sunderland before the international break was another alarm bell.

It is the first time in 67 years that Chelsea have lost at home to both Leeds and Spurs in the same season.

"We need to find solutions, for sure, because there will be setbacks during any game," Alonso said after the match.

"To be able to go through that and to know that it's still so long to play, it's something mandatory in this competition and today I felt that probably we are in a fragile moment mentally.

"When we received a punch we didn't recover that strongly."

Indeed, even when Chelsea have been winning matches, they have often looked unconvincing.

Yet Blues supporters chanted their new manager's name and seemed optimistic after the summer transfer business - despite a disappointing 10th-place finish last season.

Club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers was joined by the experienced trio of Emiliano Martinez, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson.

It was the clinical finishing of Rogers, along with Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro earlier in the season, that masked the underlying fragility of Alonso's team.

Before this weekend, the Blues ranked 14th for expected goal difference and were joint 12th in Opta's expected points table.

After their latest setback, ex-England forward and BBC Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer said: "Chelsea were all over the place. Once Moises Caicedo went off injured early on, there was no physicality and they looked weak.

"They hardly created anything going forward and the back four didn't look comfortable. There was no desire, cohesion or fight from the home side, but we shouldn't take anything away from Leeds.

"Two weeks ago Chelsea were bullied by Sunderland centre-forward Brian Brobbey and they let Dominic Calvert-Lewin do the same today, which is alarming.

"It's fair to say Xabi Alonso's honeymoon period is over. He needs to tell his players this simply isn't good enough. They are miles off it and have to do better in every department."

In Alonso's defence, Chelsea had problems before his arrival.

They finished 10th last season, having been outrun in 37 of their 38 matches, and had three managers during a chaotic campaign.

Remarkably, Chelsea have seven more points from corresponding fixtures this season and last, but it mostly serves to show how low the bar was set.

Champions League qualification was again the club's pre-season target and Alonso's appointment was designed to bring stability and authority.

The former Real Madrid and Liverpool midfielder had an impressive playing career and earned much early admiration as a manager, guiding Bayer Leverkusen to a league and cup double in 2024.

However, the Spaniard, who was sacked by Real Madrid last season, has yet to establish any real consistency - beyond his defence leaking goals regularly.

Only Crystal Palace, Coventry City and Ipswich Town have conceded more goals than Chelsea this season.

Chelsea are also now averaging fewer than a goal per game since Joao Pedro suffered a thigh injury in training. Alongside Pedro and now Caicedo, Jorrel Hato, Maxence Lacroix, Reece James and Jamie Gittens are also injured.

It highlights how they have gained little benefit of having a season without European football.

Alonso is also beginning to face criticism from sections of the fanbase for both his team selections and substitutions.

Chief among the reasons is the constant chopping and changing of the starting XI, having now made 28 line-up changes (behind only Tottenham) while also switching between back-four and back-three systems.

In addition, Alonso is being criticised for his use of personnel, having deployed Pedro Neto as a striker on two occasions and, some would argue, not made enough use of exciting young winger Estevao.

Against Leeds he gave striker Emmanuel Emegha his first start alongside Estevao and, although the Dutch striker scored, the pair were the first players he substituted while Chelsea were chasing the game at 3-1 down.

Similarly, his late in-game interventions are under scrutiny, including the decision to bring on striker Welbeck only in the 90th minute of the defeat by Spurs.

He took until the 64th minute to make changes against Leeds when Chelsea were already 3-1 down. Only three clubs had made more substitutions in the last 15 minutes than Chelsea in the league this season.

Given Leeds' strengths, Chelsea should have been better prepared for what was coming. Before kick-off, Leeds had applied more high-intensity pressures in the opposition half than any other team in the Premier League.

They had also generated the most expected goals from set-pieces and won the most duels. Leeds maintained those trends at Stamford Bridge against a Chelsea side often accused of being soft.

Chelsea have had problems in recent seasons, but this was still their worst home defeat since a 4-1 loss to Brentford in 2022.

Likewise, it is almost uncharted territory in Alonso's managerial career, having only previously lost at home by a three-goal margin once.

The stadium emptied and supporters again left early.

Players displayed negative body language and argued with one another both during the match and after the final whistle.

As a result, Alonso has gone from needing to fix defensive issues to dealing with problems that appear to be spreading throughout the squad.

SportsTab.title: Lionel Messi at center of red-card controversy as Inter Miami face early MLS playoff exit
SportsTab.text:
Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.

Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.

Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois said afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.

“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”

Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.

“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.

Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.

The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.

The result means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, can eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in Game 2 of the best-of-three series in Ohio next Friday.

“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Miami coach Kily González said afterwards.

“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out.

“There’s no better challenge for us as a team than this. It’s a test of character, and I know my team has that character.”

FC Dallas 3-0 Portland Timbers

Joaquín Valiente scored twice in the space of two minutes as FC Dallas beat the Portland Timbers 3-0 in the opening game of their best-of-three Western Conference first-round series.

The 25-year-old Uruguayan midfielder broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, volleying home a rebound after Daniel Job’s shot was parried by Portland goalkeeper James Pantemis.

Valiente doubled the lead two minutes later, timing his run to meet another pass from Job before redirecting the ball between Pantemis’s legs.

Samuel Sarver completed the scoring in the fourth minute of stoppage time, finishing a cross from Logan Farrington on the counterattack.

Dallas goalkeeper Daniel de Sousa Britto, known simply as Daniel, made four saves, while Pantemis finished with five for Portland.

The Timbers also lost Ariel Lassiter to an apparent injury in the 33rd minute.

Second-seeded Dallas can advance to the Western Conference semi-finals with a victory in Portland next Saturday.

New England Revolution 2-0 Philadelphia Union

Teenager Peyton Miller scored one goal and helped create another as the New England Revolution beat the Philadelphia Union 2-0 in the opening game of their Eastern Conference first-round series.

The 19-year-old Miller became the fifth-youngest goalscorer in MLS Cup playoffs history when he volleyed home a cross from Jack Harrison in the 73rd minute, his effort bouncing off the crossbar and into the net.

New England had taken the lead in the 10th minute when Miller’s shot from the edge of the penalty area deflected off Philadelphia defender Nathan Harriel for an own goal.

Harrison, who came on as a substitute in the 62nd minute, was making his first appearance since 9 September after missing more than two months with a quadriceps injury.

Philadelphia nearly equalized in the 37th minute when Cavan Sullivan turned and fired a shot from outside the penalty area that struck the left post.

The Union fielded the youngest starting lineup in MLS Cup playoffs history, with an average age of 23 years and 207 days, breaking the record set by the New York Red Bulls in 2022.

Matt Turner made two saves to preserve the shutout for New England, who can advance to the Eastern Conference semi-finals with a victory in Philadelphia next Saturday.

SportsTab.title: Raya injured but Madueke rescues point for Arsenal in seesaw Newcastle draw
SportsTab.text:
If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.

Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside, where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back commendably to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance. At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and subtle tactical rejig suggested he is no mug after all.

It left Arsenal – who lost their outstanding goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City, and Arteta with a face like thunder.

Just last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players. Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending about £275m this summer, they have struggled to replace last season’s departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

That reality perhaps left Howe’s successor – who arrived just before the start of the season – making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were close-season signings.

The other five new faces were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man matchday squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given Bamba and Toure cost a combined £78.5m, their omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to bench González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tag.

Meanwhile the jury remains out on Hornicek. The Czech international has made some excellent saves this season but, initially here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved after hesitating too long as the impressive Kai Havertz closed in.

Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved well apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left-back Lewis Hall given a thorough work out by Noni Madueke.

Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, endeavoured to slow the tempo but the red tide could only be stemmed for so long.

When Havertz dispossessed Hall after the latter miscontrolled a long ball, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated, pass across to the on-rushing Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance and unleashed a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past Hornicek.

As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.

With Declan Rice always available to reinforce his defence and smother any flickering home attack it proved a struggle to recall Newcastle making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box. Fans stationed near the home dugouts told Jaissle what they thought of it all.

Arsenal’s pressing was initially so good that Newcastle were left almost incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.

Yet that seemingly ambitious vision was something Harvey Barnes proved fully capable of buying into. When, early in the second half, Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch sliced the ball in Osula’s direction and the Dane played it into Barnes’s path.

All that remained was for the left winger to take a single, steadying, touch before an assured finish left the hitherto redundant David Raya picking his shot out of the net.

Jaissle’s second-half introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.

The home side were closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead when a Hall corner was headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.

Shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring Guimarães’s exit.

Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counterattacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying two defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.

No matter; Jaissle had done enough to win plenty of hearts and minds. Not least the chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan, over from Riyadh to watch his first match of the season and reportedly “take the club’s temperature”.

SportsTab.title: ‘GO NAVY’ becomes ‘GO ARMY’ after overnight prank at Navy football stadium
SportsTab.text:
The large letters that spell “GO NAVY” in the upper seating level of the Naval Academy’s football stadium were changed to “GO ARMY” in an elaborate overnight prank before the Midshipmen hosted No 24 Memphis on Saturday.

The stunt involved rearranging the blue and yellow seat backs at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium in Annapolis, Maryland, a task made considerably more complicated by the fact that the seats are bolted into place.

The letters were back to normal well before the noon kickoff. A Navy spokesperson said security footage showed uniformed Army cadets in the stadium between 1am and 4am.

According to the Athletic, stadium workers began restoring the original message at 6am, completing the job before the gates opened to spectators four hours later. Navy reportedly regarded the operation as a successful rivalry prank and did not expect any legal repercussions.

A member of ESPN’s TV broadcast team posted a picture on social media at 10.19am with the explanation: “Not AI ... 20 staff members have been working for the last couple of hours to fix the seat backs. Army Navy rivalry heating up already.”

The stunt was the latest chapter in a decades-long tradition of elaborate practical jokes between the two military academies, known as “spirit missions”, which have frequently involved the theft of each other’s mascots.

In 1991, Navy midshipmen made off with four of Army’s mule mascots, while Army cadets have repeatedly targeted Navy’s goat, Bill. A 2021 raid famously resulted in the wrong goat being taken. The academies signed an agreement in 1992 intended to put an end to mascot thefts, although the tradition has proved difficult to stamp out.

In 2022, Navy personnel flew three small aircraft over the West Point campus, scattering ping-pong balls bearing pro-Navy slogans along with leaflets.

The overnight incursion did little to spoil Navy’s Saturday. The Midshipmen upset Memphis 38-34, improving to 4-6 after entering the game with just three victories in nine outings.

Navy face Army on 12 December in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

SportsTab.title: Alcaraz holds off Shelton to set up final showdown with Zverev at ATP Finals
SportsTab.text:
The man himself was not present in Turin on Saturday afternoon, but one of the most intriguing developments on and off court in men’s tennis this year was Ben Shelton’s surprise decision to hire the former world No 1 Juan Carlos Ferrero as his new coach alongside his father, Bryan. Ferrero is one of the most highly respected coaches on tour, but he also knows Carlos Alcaraz better than any other coach in the world.

However, there is only so much that anyone can do against one of the sport’s greatest talents. Shelton, the third seed, played a spectacular match, serving monstrously, attacking without hesitation and volleying well in decisive moments, but it still wasn’t enough to defeat the second seeded Alcaraz, who maintained his focus after an uncertain start as he reached the final of the ATP Finals with a 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (1) win.

The indoor hard court swing has long been the most difficult part of the season for Alcaraz, both because of his difficulties with fatigue at the end of a long year and his relative vulnerability in faster conditions. However, at the end of a turbulent 2026 he has made significant progress indoors. Alcaraz will face Alexander Zverev, the world No 1, in the final after the German reached the final with a 7-6 (0), 6-4 win against Daniil Medvedev.

Zverev, a two-time ATP Finals champion, is yet to drop a set or concede a service game in Turin, with the rapid conditions further fortifying his enormous serve. Despite a tight opening set, Medvedev failed to generate a single break point in their 88 minutes on court.

This will mark Zverev’s first meeting with Alcaraz since he won his first two grand slam titles this year, at Roland Garros and the US Open. In their last meeting, Alcaraz dramatically defeated Zverev in five sets at the Australian Open in January.

One of the interesting developments of this indoor season has been the continued trend of hard courts across the tour speeding up. Paris and Turin represent two of the fastest courts of the past decade and these are exactly the conditions a big server like Shelton would prefer against Alcaraz. However, Alcaraz’s level has been supreme throughout this tournament.

After his loss to Shelton at the quarter-finals of the US Open two months ago, one issue Alcaraz felt he needed to address was the quality of his serve. He made a number of changes to his action once he returned home, particularly simplifying the start of his motion to find greater balance and lowering his toss. After starting slowly and conceding his opening service game, the quality of Alcaraz’s serve was perhaps the defining point of the match.

It improved throughout the match and by the final set he simply did not seem at risk of losing his serve. That security behind his first serve allowed him to start the final set tie-break completely relaxed. After Shelton fired down an ace on the first point, Alcaraz immediately followed him with two unreturned serves. While the Spaniard’s confidence skyrocketed, a forehand error from Shelton and a rare missed volley on consecutive service points quickly sealed his fate.

Despite ending his year with a defeat and understandable frustration about his wasteful errors at the close, Shelton played an excellent match. Along with his monstrous serving, the most impressive part of his performance was his netplay. Time and time again, he made excellent volleys on key points, particularly on his serve in the final set.

Shelton still has very clear weaknesses that he must continue to work on, but he ends 2026 having put together by far the best season of his career. His highlights included a first grand slam final at the US Open, four titles including the Montreal ATP 1000, and the solidification of his position as the world No 4.

This match was accompanied by ample intrigue. The added dynamic of Ferrero’s presence in Shelton’s team now makes their matches a must-watch but there were also questions over Alcaraz’s fitness after he felt pain in his left thigh during his win over Medvedev on Wednesday. Alcaraz had an MRI scan after that match.

SportsTab.title: Russell lashes out at Verstappen after Las Vegas GP clash: ‘He’s screwing all of us’
SportsTab.text:
George Russell has condemned Max Verstappen with a damning indictment of his driving at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, saying the Dutchman was “screwing” other drivers and that the four-time world champion believed he was “bigger and better than everyone else”.

After the pair came together on the street circuit during the final practice session on Friday, Russell had clearly had enough with Verstappen’s approach at overtaking him while he was preparing for a flying lap.

“There’s nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this you are screwing this person over and he does this week-in, week-out with many drivers and everybody accepts it,” Russell said.

“I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy.”

The clash in Las Vegas was investigated by the stewards where they banged wheels at turn 14 in final practice. Verstappen had overtaken Russell on the way into the corner then slowed down in front of him and, according to the FIA stewards’ decision, then changed direction. The move broke what is understood to be a gentleman’s agreement between drivers not to overtake on the warm up to a flying lap. Russell reciprocated by ducking back up the inside and the pair bashed wheels.

The Red Bull driver accused Russell of trying to push him into the barriers, while the British driver’s race engineer, Marcus Dudley said he had seen the Dutchman “cut in front of you”. After an investigation by the FIA Verstappen was found responsible and given a warning by the stewards but no penalty.

After qualifying – with Verstappen taking pole and Russell alongside him following a penalty that pushed Kimi Antonelli back to sixth on the grid – there was a frosty atmosphere between the pair. Verstappen was not even willing to address the incident. “Nothing. Nothing happened,” he said, adding when pressed on the matter: “I don’t even want to waste my time on that. It’s not worth it to me at all.”

Russell was equally stony-faced. “No confusion. I mean, it was pretty clear, I think,” he said of his outburst.

There is little love lost between the pair. In 2024 before the Qatar GP Russell said Verstappen had threatened to “put me on my fucking head in the wall” after the Dutchman lost pole position having been penalised for impeding Russell.

The British driver said at the time: “I’m not going to sit here and accept it. People have been bullied by Max for years now . You can’t question his driving abilities [but] he cannot deal with adversity whenever anything has gone against him.”

Last year Russell insisted that Verstappen should have faced disqualification after he crashed into the British driver at the Spanish GP, claiming he felt he had done so deliberately and that he was setting a bad example for young drivers.

Verstappen was bullish after a race where he received a 10-second penalty that dropped him from fifth at the flag to 10th, dismissed Russell’s comments, maintaining he had no regrets and mocking the British driver’s reactions with the comment: “Well, I’ll bring some tissues next time.” The penalty cost Verstappen nine points and he went on to lose the world championship to McLaren’s Lando Norris by two points.

In qualifying, Antonelli was only denied pole by a grid penalty. A five-place sanction for taking a new engine means Verstappen starts from the front of the grid in Nevada.

Russell, meanwhile, was clear he would have talks with Mercedes to discuss why, with the slipstream proving vital in Las Vegas, they did not engage the Italian for a tow given they knew he faced a grid drop. Antonelli still has every chance on Sunday, but it is Russell and Verstappen who hold the advantage.

In contrast, Ferrari floundered, forced to fold before even the final hand at a race where they enjoy huge support. Lewis Hamilton was struggling with a lack of grip and could not hook up a good lap. Neither he nor his teammate, Charles Leclerc, made it out of Q2, with Leclerc finishing in 11th and Hamilton 12th. They will start from 10th and 11th after McLaren’s Oscar Piastri also received a 10-place penalty for taking a new engine.

The impact of the new regulations threw an unexpected curveball into the mix at the Las Vegas Strip circuit, where the active aerodynamics of the straight-line mode proved to have a major impact on the long straight. Riding in the slipstream of a car in front was far more of an advantage than had been expected and it led to some jostling beneath the lights.

By the time to take the decisive runs arrived it was clear a tow was proving hugely beneficial. Verstappen, who had been squarely in the slipstream of his teammate, Isack Hadjar, was up by almost three-tenths on his first quick lap in Q3 to take provisional pole but Mercedes were using no such tactics and nor had Ferrari.

Russell then specifically asked the team if he could have a tow from Antonelli given the Italian had a grid penalty, a request that fell on closed ears.

As the field hustled for position for the final runs, with no driver wanting to be at the front, Antonelli decided to take a chance. He backed out and dropped to the back of the pack, losing time in the process. It was an immensely close run thing for the Italian, he was in the slipstream of all the other cars but in dropping back crossed the line to start his last lap with barely a second to spare.

It proved inspired, as he took the top spot with a time of 1min 33.893sec, two and half tenths up on Verstappen after a session where he had been far from comfortable.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
TechnologyTab.text:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

TechnologyTab.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
TechnologyTab.text:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

Upstart says it is tackling that issue.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".

As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.

"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."

Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.

Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.

"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.

"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.
